items.title: Dish with a scale motif and scrolls
items.alt_neutral: Round glazed ceramic dish seen from above: two curved white-and-red leaf shapes frame a small flower on a ground of blue and green overlapping scales; the rim is filled with blue spiral cloud motifs; small chips along the edge
items.caption: Glazed dish with curved leaves, a flower and coloured scales

journey_fact.text: Documented from 1917, when collector Julius Wilhelm Edwin vom Rath lent it to the Rijksmuseum; he bequeathed it with 305 other objects in 1941. Earlier owners and how it left Turkey are not documented.

facts.text: It is made of quartz-frit ware (a quartz-based ceramic body) with glaze, not ordinary clay earthenware.

photo.author: Rijksmuseum
photo.pd_basis: Anonymous Iznik potter, c. 1565-1585; no copyright in the object.

conflicts: No Wikidata item found for this object (searched inventory number BK-NM-12415 and title).

items.title: Vienna Dioscurides (De materia medica, Cod. Med. gr. 1)
items.alt_neutral: Large open parchment book: the left page shows a painted leafy plant with trailing roots and bright orange lantern-shaped pods; the right page carries lines of brown capital-letter script; small cursive notes in other hands at the tops of the pages
items.caption: Open parchment book with a painted plant and columns of script

made.note: Made in Byzantine Constantinople for the aristocrat Anicia Juliana

when.label: Byzanz, um 512 (about 512)
when.note: ÖNB catalogue: about 512; its blog: early 6th century; its 2019 display label: about 500

journey_fact.text: Habsburg envoy Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq found it in Constantinople with Hamon, physician to Sultan Süleyman, but did not buy it at once because of the cost; he later pressed for its purchase. In Vienna's court library by 1576.

facts.text: It was dedicated to the Roman aristocrat Anicia Juliana; a dedication picture thanks her for building a church of Mary in Honoratae, a suburb of Constantinople, in 512/513.
It copies the plant book of the Greek physician Dioscorides (1st century CE); notes in several languages translating the plant names show centuries of use. UNESCO listed it in 1997.

photo.author: Isiwal, via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Byzantine manuscript of the early 6th century; no copyright in the object
photo.crop_note: Crop 0,0,0.11,0 (cut the bottom 11%): removes the ÖNB exhibition label at lower right; trims a sliver off the book's lower edge

conflicts: Dates within the ÖNB: catalogue records 'Byzanz, um 512', the blog 'Anfang des 6. Jh.', and the 2019 display label (visible in the photo) 'vermutlich um 500 in Konstantinopel'. The range 500-512 covers the ÖNB's dates; the label's 'vermutlich' hedges, but the blog states Constantinople without a hedge.
Wikidata Q699363: inception 6th century (century precision), consistent; no location of creation (P1071).

items.title: Bowl with the monogram of Emperor Leo I
items.alt_neutral: Shallow polished silver bowl seen from above: four broad engraved bands form a cross radiating from a small central medallion holding a monogram of linked letters; double engraved lines circle the rim; a small hole near the top edge
items.caption: Polished silver bowl engraved with a cross and a central monogram

made.note: Mia credits the maker as 'Byzantine Empire (Constantinople)'

journey_fact.text: Made in Constantinople; how and when it left is not documented on Mia's record. The Minneapolis Institute of Art acquired it with funds from the Morse Foundation (accession number 68.9.1).

facts.text: The bowl bears the monogram of Emperor Leo I; Mia dates it 457-474.
It is made of silver and measures about 17.8 cm across and 4.4 cm high.

photo.author: Minneapolis Institute of Art
photo.pd_basis: Eastern Roman (Byzantine) silver of 457-474; Mia rights_type 'Public Domain': 'Artwork is in the public domain. Images are available for any use.'

conflicts: No Wikidata item found (searched P195 Q1700481 with P217 '68.9.1').

Mia's record has no place-of-creation field; the place comes from its maker field 'Byzantine Empire (Constantinople)' and the alternative maker name 'Byzantine Empire (Constantinople) [Turkey, Istanbul]'. Mia also tags nationality 'Roman' and country 'Turkey'.

items.title: Annunciation
items.alt_neutral: Long horizontal painting on wood: in a walled garden a kneeling winged figure in a red robe and pale sleeves raises two fingers and holds a white lily toward a seated young woman in a blue mantle, who lifts one hand from a book on a carved marble lectern; tall dark trees, a misty harbour and pale mountains lie beyond the low wall
items.caption: Painting of a kneeling winged figure greeting a woman at a lectern

made.note: Painted while Leonardo still worked in Verrocchio's Florence workshop

when.label: 1472 c. (Uffizi page); ca. 1472-ca. 1475 (Uffizi catalogue record)
when.note: The Uffizi page says about 1472, its catalogue record about 1472-1475; any year from 1472 to 1475 scores full marks.

journey_fact.text: Kept in the sacristy of the Olivetan church of San Bartolomeo a Monteoliveto, outside Porta San Frediano in Florence, until it came to the Uffizi in 1867. Its original location and patron are not documented.

facts.text: Until it reached the Uffizi in 1867 it was credited to Ghirlandaio; the scholar Liphart first gave it to Leonardo, and the attribution was long debated.
The Virgin's right arm looks too long, perhaps because the panel was painted to be seen from below and to the right, over a side altar in a church.

photo.author: Gallerie degli Uffizi (Google Art Project), via Wikimedia Commons
photo.pd_basis: Leonardo da Vinci died 1519; Commons tags the file PD-Art (PD-old-100-expired)

conflicts: Date: the Uffizi web page gives '1472 c.' (its video title '1472-1475 ca.'); the Uffizi catalogue record (ICCD 0900285888) gives ca. 1472-ca. 1475 with other datings 1478/1480; Wikidata Q1217213 P571 gives circa 1472. The range 1472-1475 covers the museum's own dates; the 1478/1480 alternatives are listed by the record as other opinions, not used.

Provenance: Wikidata P276 gives the Territorial Abbey of Monte Oliveto Maggiore (Siena) until 1876 and the Uffizi from 1876; the Uffizi says San Bartolomeo a Monteoliveto in Florence, arriving 1867. The museum is used.

Attribution: the Uffizi catalogue record lists Ridolfo del Ghirlandaio, Verrocchio and Lorenzo di Credi with Leonardo as other attributions and calls it generally a collaboration of Verrocchio's workshop and Leonardo; the Uffizi page names Leonardo.
